source.title: AOS: Adaptive Optimizer Switching via Training-State Signals for Faster Convergence and Better Generalization
source.authors: A. K. Pandey; Umang Chaturvedi; A. Rana; Gopi Krishna Nedanuri

record.tranche_reason: Reports its own comparison of adaptive and non-adaptive optimizer training and argues the generalization outcome depends on training phase, switching policy, and architecture. The results refine the optimizer comparison in V4, but do not test V1–V3 or V5–V8.
record.gate_note: Rows capture the paper's own optimizer comparisons and switching ablations that report validation accuracy or convergence speed. Cited SWATS findings and signal values used only to trigger switches are not rows. The study does not measure the training-to-test gap or compare training performance.
record.test_reason: Table II contains direct standalone AdamW, Lion and momentum-SGD comparisons of held-out accuracy, bearing on V4 independently of AOS's performance. Training error is unnecessary for that comparison, but the paper does not establish the limited-tuning restriction or the equal-training-performance clause.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase largely captures the authors' conclusion: six of eight AOS-R accuracy wins, faster milestones, and PyramidNet failures. Qualify their aggregate claims: Table II's +0.4 pp summarizes the six wins over the best baseline, not an eight-task gain over AdamW. SE-ResNet-32/CIFAR-100 improves by 0.6 pp over the best baseline, despite the text claiming 0.9 pp. The authors call results single-seed although Table IV reports three seeds. Figure 3 says all methods finish near 79%, conflicting with the conclusion's sustained 2–3 pp advantage and Table IV's 82.2% full-controller result.
record.recipe_differences: Trains CIFAR image classifiers with a signal-driven switching controller among AdamW, SGD-M and Lion, using state transfer and a learning-rate bridge; standalone baselines use publication hyperparameters validated by grid search. It does not compare the fixed recipes specified in V4.
record.method_sensitivity: Architecture changes the outcome: AOS-R trails SGD-M on PyramidNet-110 for CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100. The CIFAR-100/WRN-28-10 ablations also report performance changes with signal choices, dwell calibration, transition-state handling, and bridge use.

fits_no_version.finding: AOS-R wins six of eight main accuracy comparisons but loses to SGD-M on both PyramidNet tasks; controller ablations measure sensitivity to signals, dwell, state transfer and optimizer order.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A signal-driven multi-optimizer controller can improve validation accuracy, with architecture-dependent failures and configuration sensitivity.

fits_no_version.finding: AOS reaches accuracy targets faster and leads during early training.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Optimizer switching can accelerate convergence to validation-accuracy milestones.

record.problems: The study reports only best validation accuracy and convergence speed, not training error or a train-test gap; therefore it cannot establish the central generalization-gap claim. Most main comparisons are single-seed. The three-seed ablation is only on CIFAR-100/WRN-28-10. ImageNet and GLUE evaluations are stated to be in progress.
record.rows_left_out: Table III per-optimizer convergence-speed values are included as comparator rows R10–R17, but they cannot determine V4's held-out generalization claim. Other detailed Table IV ablation values and speed entries were not added because the flattened layout does not reliably pair every condition and value; the study's own summary states major ablation effects in Section VI, but they do not measure the train-test gap. Figure-only accuracy curves and signal traces were not transcribed as numeric rows.

untested.parts: Convolutional versus fully connected architectures and local connectivity.

Restriction to learning-rate and schedule tuning is not established: grid-search dimensions and budgets are unspecified. No training-performance comparison, language benchmarks, tuning-budget intervention, or controlled Adam-versus-AdamW comparison. Multiway AOS ablations do not isolate simple Adam-to-SGD recovery.
Batch-size comparisons and remedies under fixed epoch budgets.
Dropout interventions and joint dropout/weight-decay removal.
Magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance, measured generalization gaps, and ranking against competing measures.
Removal of memorized versus random training examples.

record.verdict_notes: Only the supplied text was used. The original extraction incorrectly treats absence of training-error measurements as preventing any V4 test. Held-out standalone comparisons suffice for V4's performance clause. Main comparisons are single-seed, tuning dimensions are unspecified, and small differences have no reported uncertainty.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label test generalization coexistence.
Generalization as network width increases beyond interpolation.
Convolutional versus fully connected image generalization.

Limited-tuning adaptive-optimizer comparisons on language benchmarks; broader tuning, decoupled weight decay, switching from Adam to SGD in isolation, and word-level language models. The paper uses grid-searched task-specific baselines and tests an adaptive switching scheme, not the isolated optimizer comparisons in the full version.
Large-batch effects under fixed epoch budgets.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its relationship to the train-test gap.
Effect of removing memorized training examples.

relationships.condition: ResNet, DenseNet and PyramidNet standalone comparisons on CIFAR-10/100; 200 epochs, seed 42, publication hyperparameters validated by task-specific grid search
relationships.reason: R1, R3, R5, R6 and R7 show AdamW trailing SGD-M by 0.3–2.7 pp and Lion by 0.6–1.2 pp; these support the adaptive-performance disadvantage in these tested recipes.
relationships.display_finding: Reported AdamW and Lion accuracies trail momentum SGD, but these single-seed comparisons remain unverified.

relationships.reason: R2 shows only a 0.2 pp disadvantage for both AdamW and Lion versus SGD-M, with no multi-seed uncertainty.
relationships.display_finding: AdamW and Lion reportedly trailed SGD-M by 0.2 percentage points, but this comparison remains unverified and lacked uncertainty across seeds.

relationships.condition: SE-ResNet-32 on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100, standalone optimizers
relationships.reason: R4 and R8 show AdamW exceeding SGD-M by 0.2 pp on both datasets; Lion exceeds it by 0.1 pp on CIFAR-10 and trails by 0.1 pp on CIFAR-100. The disadvantage depends on architecture and optimizer.
relationships.display_finding: AdamW reportedly exceeded SGD-M on both datasets while Lion's direction varied, but these comparisons remain unverified.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: AOS-R outscored standalone optimizer baselines on six of eight combinations, but SGD-M scored higher on PyramidNet-110 for both datasets (R1–R8). The paper reports a mean +0.4 pp gain and 0.80× aggregate convergence speed relative to AdamW (R9). These results concern a switching method and validation performance, not a direct measurement of the training-to-test gap.
